evidence_summary: Hanbali is the institutionally predominant madhhab; the country's population also includes many residents/citizens of other madhahib in practice, so this is a majority signal, not a certainty.
sources: RSRC-012: 2020 Report on International Religious Freedom: Saudi Arabia (U.S. Department of State (via hrvoices.org), 2020) https://hrvoices.org/assets/attachments/documents/240282-SAUDI-ARABIA-2020-INTERNATIONAL-RELIGIOUS-FREEDOM-REPORT.pdf | RSRC-013: "Precarious Justice" (Human Rights Watch, March 2008) https://www.hrw.org/reports/2008/saudijustice0308/5.htm
reviewer_notes: The single strongest case in the whole dataset: a directly-quotable US State Dept report explicitly ties the legal system, the Council of Senior Scholars' seat allocation, and public education to the Hanbali school by name.

evidence_summary: Maliki is the historically and institutionally predominant madhhab across the Maghreb.
sources: RSRC-001: 2023 Report on International Religious Freedom: Morocco (U.S. Department of State (via ecoi.net), 2023/2024) https://www.ecoi.net/en/document/2111925.html | RSRC-023: Les Tijanes du Mali pour un Islam tolérant et une spiritualité tirée du rite malikite (Le Courrier de l'Atlas (Mohamed El Hamraoui), 2021-07-21) https://www.lecourrierdelatlas.com/?p=174888
reviewer_notes: Morocco's own 2023 State Dept report explicitly names the 'Maliki-Ashari school'; a secondary French-language source corroborates the regional Maghreb pattern.

evidence_summary: Hanafi is the majority madhhab across South Asia generally.
sources: RSRC-006: "Memories" (Episode 43) (muftitaqiusmani.com (memoir of Mufti Muhammad Taqi Usmani, Council of Islamic Ideology member, internationally recognized Hanafi jurist), not stated) https://muftitaqiusmani.com/en/?p=13370 | RSRC-007: Religion in Pakistan (citing the Oxford Dictionary of Islam) (Oxford University Press (via Wikipedia citation trail, not independently fetched -- paywalled), not stated) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religion_in_Pakistan
reviewer_notes: A first-hand memoir by Mufti Muhammad Taqi Usmani (a longtime member of Pakistan's own Council of Islamic Ideology and internationally recognized Hanafi jurist), directly fetched and quoted: 'most of the laws came to be drafted according to the Hanafi school of thought' due to the majority population. Corroborated by a secondary citation to the Oxford Dictionary of Islam ('the majority of Sunnis follow the Hanafi school'), though that specific reference work is paywalled and was not independently fetched. Real internal nuance noted (Barelvi/Deobandi sub-division within Pakistani Hanafism; a Shia minority of ~10-20% with its own codified personal-status law since 2021) -- doesn't contradict the country-level Hanafi-Sunni-majority claim.

evidence_summary: Hanafi is the historically and institutionally predominant madhhab (Ottoman legal tradition).
sources: RSRC-018: General Assembly speech (Diyanet Academy bill debate) (Turkish Grand National Assembly (TBMM) -- official government record, 2022-03-15) https://tbmm.gov.tr/Milletvekili/UyeGenelKurulKonusmalariDetay?eid=105242 | RSRC-019: Exclusive survey looks into Turkey's religious life profile (Anadolu Agency (Turkey's state-run news agency), reporting an official Diyanet/TurkStat joint survey (37,624 households, 81 provinces, fieldwork May-Sept 2013), 2014-07-15) https://www.aa.com.tr/en/life/exclusive-survey-looks-into-turkeys-religious-life-profile/141301
reviewer_notes: An official Turkish government survey (Diyanet/TurkStat, 37,624 households, 2013) found 77.5% of Muslim citizens self-identify as Hanafi, 11.1% as Shafi'i -- a real hard percentage from an official source, not an inference. A possible Shafi'i-majority pocket in Turkish Kurdistan was mentioned only in an uncited Wikipedia sentence and could not be independently verified; flagged, not acted on.

evidence_summary: Shafi'i is the historically and institutionally predominant madhhab across maritime Southeast Asia.
sources: RSRC-036: Shāfi'ī Literature in Indonesia: A Historical Account (Islamica: Jurnal Studi Keislaman, Vol. 17 No. 1 (Suud Sarim Karimullah, Gümüşhane University), UIN Sunan Ampel, 2022-09-01) https://islamica.uinsa.ac.id/index.php/islamica/article/view/946
reviewer_notes: A peer-reviewed Indonesian academic journal article (Islamica, UIN Sunan Ampel, 2022, DOI cited) directly confirms Shafi'i's continuing reference status for Indonesian Islamic law; corroborated by convergent (but not independently re-fetched) Indonesian-university sources on Shafi'i's historical adoption as the state's official school and its 1953/1958 formal adoption for religious courts (exact year disputed between two secondary sources, a minor historical detail).

evidence_summary: Shafi'i is the predominant madhhab among Yemen's Sunni Muslim majority (roughly two-thirds of the population), concentrated in the south and along the coast.
sources: RSRC-021: 2018 Report on International Religious Freedom: Yemen (U.S. Department of State (via ecoi.net), 2018) https://www.ecoi.net/en/document/2011009.html
caveats: CORRECTED 2026-10-12: a prior version of this entry listed 'hanafi' as a second likely madhhab for the north, describing it as 'Zaydi-Hanafi-adjacent'. This was an evidence error -- Zaydism is a distinct branch of Shia Islam with its own independent legal tradition, not a variant of Sunni Hanafi jurisprudence, and has been removed from likely_madhahib accordingly. Yemen's substantial Zaydi Shia minority (historically concentrated in the northern highlands, including Sana'a) is real and significant, but is outside this app's four supported Sunni madhahib -- noted here for honesty, not folded into a guessed madhhab.
reviewer_notes: Confirms the Yemen correction made in the prior Knowledge-Base Completion wave is accurate: the 2018 State Dept report (corroborated across 2015/16/19/20/22/23 editions) names only Shafi'i and Zaydi (Shia) for Yemen, NEVER Hanafi -- the north's distinguishing feature is the Zaydi Shia minority, not a Hanafi Sunni community, confirming the earlier fix was correct.
